author.name: Voltaire
author.biography: Born François-Marie Arouet, Voltaire knew imprisonment, exile and the privileges of wealthy patrons. His writing repeatedly challenged religious intolerance and the abuse of power. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 brought the problem of innocent suffering into brutal focus, and he argued fiercely against explanations that made catastrophe part of a reassuring design. Published in 1759, Candide turns that argument into a fast, savage comedy, sending an inexperienced young man into a world his education has taught him to misunderstand.

hook.text: Do we live in the best possible world?

paragraphs: Candide has been given a reassuring education. His tutor can explain why everything is arranged for the best. It is a useful belief to carry out into the world, provided you do not look too closely at what happens there.

Voltaire looks closely, then tells the story at an outrageous speed. Armies march, disasters arrive, fortunes vanish. A character scarcely has time to recover from one calamity before the next begins. The explanations keep coming too. Almost anything can be made to fit a theory if somebody else is paying the price.
The surprise is how funny this can be. The calm sentences and confident reasoning become absurd beside the things they describe. Laughter gives us a moment's distance, then the human cost catches up.

Candide's trust makes him easy to fool, but it also gives him reasons to keep going. He wants people to be good; he wants love and a place in the world. Losing every hope would be a kind of defeat too. His companions offer other ways of meeting misfortune, from sweeping pessimism to the practical business of finding food and getting someone out of trouble.

Voltaire's targets are particular as well as philosophical: religious persecution, the glamour of war, the wealth made from other people's suffering. There are things here that should resist our appetite for a comforting explanation.
The book asks what becomes possible when we stop needing the world to prove our theory right. If an explanation for suffering leaves the sufferer exactly where they were, what has it helped us do?

orientation.text: The short chapters move quickly between countries and sudden reversals. Let the improbable pace be part of the comedy. Pangloss's confidence is a satirical target, not a dependable explanation of events.

characters.name: Candide
characters.role: An innocent young man with a reassuring education
characters.body: Raised in a baron's household, Candide has learned to trust his tutor's explanation that everything is arranged for the best. Affectionate and inexperienced, he carries that confidence into a world that gives him little reason to keep it. His hopes survive an astonishing amount of contrary evidence.

characters.name: Pangloss
characters.role: The tutor who can explain everything
characters.body: A philosopher employed in the baron's household, certain that the world forms the best possible arrangement. He is remarkably skilful at fitting experience to that conviction. His pupil's trust makes his confident explanations consequential long after the lesson has ended.

characters.name: Cunégonde
characters.body: The young woman Candide loves and one of the reasons his childhood world seems so desirable. She belongs to a household proud of its rank. The distance between the life imagined for her and the experiences she recounts gives the story another perspective on what survival costs.

characters.name: Cacambo
characters.body: Experienced, practical and quick to understand a new situation. His usefulness often becomes clear while other people are still explaining events.

characters.name: Martin
characters.body: A man whose experience has given him little confidence in human goodness. His arguments challenge Candide from the opposite direction to Pangloss.

characters.name: The old woman
characters.body: A survivor with a long story of her own. She brings practical judgment and a difficult perspective on other people's misfortunes.

characters.name: The young baron
characters.body: Proud of his family's position. Changes in circumstance do little to loosen his attachment to rank.
